messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 73
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Photos): Related photos, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room, Compulsive Spending: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself, Freeze When Threatened: freeze completely when feeling threatened
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Michael Chen

Michael Chen, seventy-three, sits in the therapy office with his back pressed firmly against the wall, his shoulders angled so that he can see the entire room and the door. He has done this automatically for so long that he no longer notices himself doing it. The journalist who once moved through rooms with the easy confidence of someone accustomed to being the observer rather than the observed now orients his body as though every space might contain a threat he needs to monitor.

Thirty-four months ago, Michael was in the Astoria Hotel in Portland covering a labor dispute for the *Oregonian*. He was in the third-floor conference room when the explosion occurred—a device planted by someone with a grudge, though the full motive was never entirely clear. The blast came without warning. Michael remembers the flash, the sound that seemed to come from inside his own body, the taste of copper and something chemical, something burning that he has never been able to identify precisely but which he tastes now when he thinks about that moment. He remembers the weight of debris. He remembers the silence afterward, which was somehow worse than the noise. He was pulled from the rubble by firefighters. Three people died in the conference room. Michael was not supposed to survive.

For the first weeks after, Michael functioned on adrenaline and the strange clarity that comes from being alive when others are not. He gave statements to authorities. He returned to his apartment in Northeast Portland. But something had fractured in him that could not be repaired by simple passage of time. The memory of those moments had taken on a quality of unreality that disturbed him more than the fear itself. When he tried to describe it to his ex-wife during one of their stilted phone calls, he found himself saying, "It doesn't feel like it really happened to me. It feels like I'm remembering a movie I watched." But it had happened. He knew this. Yet his mind could not seem to integrate the knowledge that he had been there, that his body had been crushed beneath concrete and steel, that he had tasted that chemical taste while darkness pressed down.

The memory replayed constantly. In the shower. While reading the newspaper. At three in the morning. It was like a film that his mind kept rewinding and playing again—the flash, the pressure, the taste, the silence. When the memory came, it did not feel like remembering. It felt like the explosion was happening again, right now, in the present moment. His heart would race. His breathing would become shallow. His body would freeze completely, as though any movement might trigger another collapse. He would sit motionless for minutes, unable to move or speak, waiting for the threat to pass.

Michael began to notice things. The weight of a letter opener on his desk. The angle of a picture frame. The distance to the nearest exit in any room he entered. He would scan environments automatically, cataloguing potential weapons, potential dangers. His apartment became a fortress of small rituals. He moved his chair so his back was always to the wall. He began to listen obsessively for sounds—footsteps in the hallway, the elevator arriving, someone's key in a lock. He was certain that if he was not vigilant, if he allowed his attention to lapse for even a moment, something terrible would happen again.

The triggers were specific and unpredictable. Photographs—particularly any image from the hotel, any news coverage from that day—would send him spiraling. Unpredictable situations, moments when he could not anticipate what would come next, would activate a cascading sense of dread. And certain tastes, particularly anything metallic or chemical, would transport him instantly back to the rubble.

Over the months, Michael developed strategies to manage the intolerable feeling that he was losing himself. He could not relax even in his locked apartment, even knowing rationally that he was safe. So he spent money. He would order things online—books he would not read, tools he would not use, clothes he would not wear—simply for the momentary distraction, the brief sense of agency that came from clicking "purchase." His credit card debt climbed. His apartment filled with unopened packages. But the spending worked, in a way. It interrupted the loop. It gave his mind something else to focus on.

He stopped attending journalism conferences. He turned down assignments. He could not bear the unpredictability of travel, the exposure of public spaces. After forty-two years at the *Oregonian*, he took early retirement. His editor called it a loss. Michael called it survival.

What frightened him most was the conviction that had settled into his bones: if he allowed himself to think deeply about the explosion, to really sit with it, he would not be able to handle it. He would break. And beyond that fear was something darker—the belief that he had already broken, that the capacity to feel anything normal, anything whole, had been taken from him in that moment. Nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore. His work, which had once been the organizing principle of his identity, seemed hollow. His relationships had withered. He was seventy-three years old and he was living in a world that had become a series of threats to be managed rather than a place to be inhabited.

It was his daughter who finally insisted he come. She had noticed the unopened packages, the tremor in his hands, the way he positioned himself at the edge of family dinners. She had noticed that he was disappearing. Michael came to therapy not because he believed it would help, but because his daughter asked him to, and because some part of him—a part he could barely access beneath the vigilance and the fear—wondered if there might be a way to live that did not feel like this.
